name: The Threshold
goal: Run a Python program, read its output, and say what the interpreter did with the source.

description.what: What a program actually is - a file of ordinary text - and what happens to that text when you run it.
description.why: Everything else in this dungeon is written into files like this one, and a great deal of programming is spent reading the output and the messages that come back from running them.
description.enables: You will be able to run a Python file, say in order what the interpreter did with each line, predict exactly what appears on the screen, and read an error message instead of being frightened by it.
description.assumes: Nothing at all. You have never written a line of code, and no word used here is assumed to be familiar before it is explained.
description.assessed: You will predict the exact output of small programs, put the lines of a program into the order that produces a stated result, and explain in your own words what the interpreter did - including when it stopped and why.

sections.title: A program is a piece of writing
sections.body:
A computer knows nothing and decides nothing. Left alone it does precisely as much as a kettle with no water in it. The only thing that makes it act is a list of instructions somebody wrote down, and that list, written out as ordinary text, is called **source code**. A file holding some is a **program**. There is nothing magical inside such a file: `tower.py` opened in a text editor shows the same letters, brackets and full stops you see below, and you could change any one of them with the same keystrokes you would use on a shopping list.

Source code is written for two audiences at once, and forgetting the second one is the commonest way for a working program to become an unmaintainable one. The first audience is the machine, which is merciless about spelling and punctuation and completely indifferent to whether the thing reads well. The second is the next person to open the file - very often you, months later, having forgotten every reason behind every decision. Code that satisfies only the machine is code nobody dares change.

The part written purely for that second audience is a **comment**. A `#` means *ignore the rest of this line*, so the words after it are never obeyed, never checked and never shown. They exist only to be read. A comment can occupy a whole line, or sit on the end of a line that does real work.

A useful comment says something the code cannot say for itself - why this is here, what would break without it, which awkward fact of the world forced it. A comment that merely restates the line beneath it is worse than nothing, because it is one more thing that can drift out of date and start telling lies.
sections.code:
# A greeting for anyone who reaches the top of the stair.
print("Welcome to the tower.")
print("Mind the third step.")  # it has been loose since the fire

annotations.text: A whole line given over to a comment. The machine skips it entirely; it is here so the next reader knows what this small file is for.

A comment can also follow real work on the same line. Everything from the hash to the end of the line is ignored, so the instruction in front of it is unaffected. Notice this note says WHY the step is loose, which is a fact the code itself could never carry.

checkpoint.explain: The middle line looks exactly like working code, and that is the trap: the hash in front of it puts the whole line beyond the machine's notice, so it may as well not be in the file. Switching a line off this way, rather than deleting it, is something you will do constantly.

sections.title: The interpreter, and the order it reads in
sections.body:
A file of text cannot do anything by itself. Something has to pick it up, work out what each line means, and carry it out - and for Python that something is a program called the **interpreter**. It is itself just a program, written by other people and installed on your machine, and its whole job is reading your file and acting on it. On a command line you set it going by naming it and then naming your file: `python tower.py`.

The interpreter starts at the top of the file and works downwards, one line at a time, finishing each line before it looks at the next. That sounds too obvious to be worth stating, and it is the single most useful fact on this floor. A program is not a description of a situation, the way a recipe card describes a cake; it is a sequence of moments, and the order the lines are written in is the order in which things happen.

So two files holding exactly the same three lines in different orders are different programs with different results, and neither will complain. Nothing is kept between runs, either: each time you run the file the interpreter reads it again from the top as though it had never seen it before, which is why running the same file twice gives you the same output twice.

One more consequence, worth holding on to. Nothing in the file happens while you are typing it. Writing is one act and running is another, and the gap between them is where every surprise lives.
sections.code:
print("You knock three times.")
print("A bolt slides back.")
print("The door opens.")

annotations.text: The interpreter begins here, at the first line of the file, and nowhere else.
It reaches this line only after the two above it have finished. Move it to the top and the story becomes nonsense, even though every line is still perfectly correct on its own.

checkpoint.prompt:
Arrange these three lines into a program that prints, in this order:

`Fill the lamp.`
`Light the lamp.`
`Climb the stair.`
checkpoint.explain: Each line is correct wherever it sits, so nothing here is a spelling question - the only thing that decides the answer is the order the interpreter meets the lines in, top to bottom. Programs that are wrong in this way never complain; they simply do the right things at the wrong moment.

sections.title: print, and why anything appears at all
sections.body:
Almost everything a program does is invisible. Work happens inside the machine and leaves no trace, so if you want to see something you have to ask for it, and the instruction that asks is `print`. You write the word, then round brackets, then whatever you want shown: `print("hello")`. Each `print` puts its material on the screen and then moves to a new line, so three prints make three lines.

The quotation marks matter enormously. Text inside quotes is handed over exactly as written, spaces and punctuation and all, and the quotes themselves are not part of what appears. Without quotes, Python does not see writing - it sees something to work out. So `print("2 + 3")` shows the little sum itself while `print(2 + 3)` shows `5`, and neither is a mistake; they are answers to two different requests.

`print()` with nothing between the brackets is legal and useful: it produces an empty line, which is how programs get room to breathe.

The mirror image of all this is the commonest disappointment of a first hour. A line that works something out but never prints it is not broken and does not complain - it does the work, throws the result away, and the screen stays empty. Silence is not failure. Silence nearly always means you never asked to see anything.

annotations.text: In quotes, so the characters are shown exactly as typed: 2 + 3. Nothing is worked out.
No quotes, so Python works the sum out first and shows what it comes to: 5.
The sum is worked out here too - and then discarded, because nothing asked for it to be shown. This line produces no output at all, and no complaint either.
Empty brackets produce an empty line. That is the blank line you will see between 5 and The end.

checkpoint.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line it produces.
checkpoint.explain: Two lines out of three, because the last one works its sum out and then has nowhere to put the answer. If you expected a third line you were reading `7 + 1` as a request to show the result - but showing is what `print` is for, and nothing else does it on your behalf.

sections.title: When it goes wrong, the machine tells you
sections.body:
A mistake in a program is not a disaster, damages nothing, and is not a sign that you are unsuited to this. It is the ordinary condition of writing code, including for people who have been doing it for thirty years. What happens when you make one is that the interpreter stops and prints a message describing what it could not do, and the whole skill is reading that message instead of panicking at the sight of it.

The message is called a **traceback**, and it is read from the bottom upwards. The last line names the kind of problem and describes it; the lines above it name the file and the line number where the trouble was and show you the offending text. Everything you need is in there, which is why guessing at a fix before reading it wastes so much time.

Failure arrives at one of two moments, and telling them apart is genuinely useful. Some faults are found while the program is running: the lines before the bad one have already been carried out, so their output sits above the message. The program below is like this. It prints its first line, then meets a word the interpreter has never heard of and stops, and its third line never runs at all.

The other kind is found before anything runs. If the file cannot be understood as Python at all - a quotation mark left open, a bracket never closed - the interpreter reports a **SyntaxError** and refuses to start, so not one line of the file is carried out and nothing whatever is printed. Empty output with a message about syntax means the whole file was rejected, not that the first line failed.
sections.code:
print("Opening the ledger.")
prnt("Counting the coins.")
print("Closing the ledger.")

annotations.text: This runs, and its output appears above the message. Whatever went wrong later, this line already happened.
`prnt` is a misspelling, and the interpreter has no instruction by that name, so it stops here and reports a NameError - helpfully asking whether you meant print.
Never reached. Everything stopped on the line above, so this line has no effect whatsoever, which is exactly why the output ends where it does.

checkpoint.prompt: Run the program above in your head. What appears on the screen before the error message? If nothing does, write `nothing`.
checkpoint.code:
print("Opening the ledger.")
prnt("Counting the coins.")
print("Closing the ledger.")
checkpoint.explain: One line, not none and not two: the fault is found while the program is running, so everything above it had already happened and everything below it never happens at all. A file rejected for bad syntax behaves quite differently and prints nothing whatsoever.

guided-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line it produces, including any blank ones.
guided-practice.code:
# The watchman's rounds.
print("Round one.")
print()
print("Round two.")
guided-practice.hint: Four lines in the file, but one of them is a comment and one has nothing between its brackets.
guided-practice.explain: Three lines of output from four lines of file: the comment contributes nothing at all, and the empty `print()` contributes a line with nothing on it. It is tempting to leave the blank line out because it looks like an absence, but it is a real line the program deliberately produced.

guided-practice.prompt:
The interpreter reads a file downwards, one line at a time. Arrange these lines so the program prints, in this order:

`Open the book.`
`Light the candle.`
`Read the first line.`
guided-practice.hint: The first line of output must be produced by the first line of the file.
guided-practice.explain: There is no cleverness to find here, which is the lesson: output order is file order, always. Anyone hunting for a rule that decides which line is somehow the most important is importing an idea from elsewhere - the interpreter has no such notion.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill both blanks. The program must show `Two coins left.` on the screen, and its second line must be a note for the next human reader that the interpreter ignores entirely.
guided-practice.template:
___("Two coins left.")
___ the shopkeeper counts them again at closing
guided-practice.hint: One instruction makes things appear on the screen. One character makes the rest of a line invisible to the machine.
guided-practice.explain: These are the two halves of the floor in two lines: one instruction addressed to the machine, one line addressed only to people. Notice the note carries something the code could not say for itself - what happens later, at closing time.

guided-practice.hint: Everything after a hash is ignored, wherever on the line the hash appears.
guided-practice.explain: Both `two` and `four` are hidden, but for slightly different reasons worth separating: the second line is a comment from its very start, while the third does real work first and only then falls into a comment. Perfectly good code inside a comment is still nothing but text.

guided-practice.prompt: The interpreter reads this file downwards. For each line, write what that line puts on the screen. Write `nothing` if the line puts nothing there, and `blank` if it produces an empty line.
guided-practice.hint: Take the lines strictly in order and judge each one on its own; a commented line is not skipped cleverly, it simply has nothing in it to do.
guided-practice.explain: Walking a file line by line, saying what each one does, is the technique you will fall back on for the rest of your programming life when something misbehaves. The two lines that show no text are not the same as one another: one contains nothing to obey, the other obeys an instruction whose result happens to be empty.

guided-practice.prompt:
You run a file called `ledger.py` and this comes back:

`Opening the ledger.`
`Traceback (most recent call last):`
`  File "ledger.py", line 2, in <module>`
`    prnt("Counting the coins.")`
`NameError: name 'prnt' is not defined. Did you mean: 'print'?`

Explain what the interpreter did, which line it stopped on, why that first line of output is there at all, and what you would change.
guided-practice.hint: Read the message from its bottom line upwards, and account for the output above it as well as for the line that never appeared.
guided-practice.explain: The message is not a scolding, it is a report: it names the file, the line number, the exact text it choked on and the kind of problem, and here it even guesses the fix. The output above it is evidence that line 1 had already run, which also tells you line 3 never did - the interpreter stopped at line 2 rather than skipping over it.

independent-practice.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line it produces, including any blank ones.
independent-practice.code:
print("The lantern is out.")
print()
# print("The lantern is lit.")
print("It is dark.")  # nothing to see by
independent-practice.answer:
The lantern is out.

It is dark.
independent-practice.explain: Four lines of file, three lines of output, and the middle one is empty. Getting this exactly right - blank line included, hidden line excluded - is the whole of what this floor asks, because output is a precise thing rather than a rough impression.

independent-practice.prompt: A friend sends you a file named `tally.py` and says it does not work: she double-clicked it, a black window flashed up and vanished, and now she thinks the file is broken. Explain what that file actually is, what has to happen to it before anything can occur at all, and what you would ask her to try instead.
independent-practice.explain: The file is inert - it is writing, and writing does nothing until something reads it. The flash of the window is the giveaway: her machine did hand the file to the interpreter, which read it from the top, printed whatever it printed, finished, and took the window with it. Nothing was broken; the output simply had nowhere to stay, which is what a command line is for.

independent-practice.prompt:
A whole file contains exactly these two lines:

`2 + 3`
`"hello"`

Running it produces no message of any kind and shows nothing on the screen. Somebody concludes that Python is broken, or that the file never ran. Explain what really happened, and what would have to change for anything to appear.
independent-practice.explain: Both lines were carried out perfectly - the sum was worked out, the text was looked at - and both results were thrown away, because nothing asked for either of them to be shown. The absence of any message is the clue that nothing went wrong: a program that succeeds silently and a program that fails look nothing alike, because failure always says so.

independent-practice.prompt:
Arrange these four lines into a file that produces exactly this output, in this order:

`Cellar door.`
`It is locked.`

`Try the window.`
independent-practice.explain: The blank line in the wanted output is not decoration, it is a line the program has to produce deliberately, and only the empty fragment can produce it. Reading the wanted output as three lines rather than four is how this one goes wrong.

independent-practice.prompt: Two people write a note above the same line of a program. The line is `print("Mind the third step.")`. One writes `# print the message about the third step`; the other writes `# the step has been loose since the fire and visitors keep tripping`. Say what the next reader gains from each of them, which one you would delete, and why.
independent-practice.explain: The first note tells the reader only what the line beneath it already says out loud, so it earns nothing and costs something: change that line later and the note quietly becomes a lie. The second carries a fact that appears nowhere in the code and could not be recovered from it - and facts the code cannot state are precisely what comments are for.

choices: A program that reads a file of Python source code and carries out its instructions.
The window in which the output of a program appears.
A file containing the text of a program.
The part of the computer that stores files while it is switched off.
exam.explain: It is a program, no more mysterious than the one you are writing, whose particular job is reading yours. Confusing it with the window is easy, because that is where you see its work - but the same window would show the output of anything at all.

The two visible lines arrive by quite different routes - the first is text copied out exactly, the second is a sum worked out first - and they happen to end in the same characters, which is why the quotation marks are worth watching. The third line is hidden regardless of what it says.

exam.prompt: Fill the blanks so this file prints `Ready.` and then an empty line, and so its last line is a note the interpreter never obeys.
exam.template:
print("___")
___()
___ remember to check the lamp oil before setting off
exam.explain: The full stop belongs inside the quotes, because text is reproduced exactly as written and a missing full stop is therefore different output. Empty brackets are the only way to ask for a line with nothing on it.

exam.prompt: Give the number of lines that have appeared on the screen once the interpreter has finished each of these lines.
exam.explain: The count rises for the empty print and not for the comment, which is the distinction this whole floor turns on: one line produces something you cannot see, the other produces nothing at all. Treating those two as the same thing is the mistake the question exists to catch.

exam.prompt:
Arrange these lines into a file whose output is exactly:

`Sweep the hearth.`
`Lay the fire.`
`Strike the match.`
exam.explain: Every line is faultless on its own, so nothing here can be judged by looking at a single line - only the sequence can be wrong. That is the characteristic shape of an ordering fault, and it is why such faults never announce themselves with a message.

exam.prompt:
A file has four lines. The first two are ordinary instructions that show text on the screen. On the third line a quotation mark was left unclosed. Running the file produces no output at all, followed by this:

`  File "bells.py", line 3`
`    print("The bell rings again.`
`SyntaxError: unterminated string literal (detected at line 3)`

Explain why the first two lines produced nothing, even though there is nothing wrong with them.
exam.explain: This failure happens at the earlier of the two moments: the interpreter must be able to make sense of the whole file before it carries out any of it, so a fault of this kind means nothing ever started. That is why the empty output is informative rather than mysterious - had the first two lines run and something gone wrong afterwards, their output would be sitting above the message.

exam.prompt: You run the same file on Monday and again on Friday and get identical output both times. A colleague says the computer has remembered the program from Monday. Say what actually happens on Friday, from the moment you ask for the file to be run.
exam.explain: Nothing is kept between runs: the file is read again from the top as though for the first time, and the output is identical only because the text is identical. This matters more than it sounds - it is why editing the file changes Friday's result, and why a program that behaves differently on two runs must be getting something from outside the file.

exam.prompt: Which of these are true of a comment in a Python file?
choices: It begins at a hash and runs to the end of that line.
It is ignored by the interpreter.
It is printed on the screen when the program runs.
It may follow an instruction on the same line.
It must occupy a line of its own.
exam.explain: The two false statements come from the same misunderstanding - that a comment is part of what the program does. It is never shown and it need not stand alone; it is a note that stops at the end of its line, and nowhere else.

exam.prompt: What does this program print? Write every line it produces, including any blank ones.
exam.explain: Five lines of file, four lines of output: one blank, one piece of text that merely looks like a sum, one sum that really was worked out, and one line whose result went nowhere. A fifth line would mean you were assuming the last line shows itself, which is the habit this floor exists to break.
